clue.text: Group's accountant acquiring some doubtful money

blocks.note: CA is a chartered accountant
boodle is slang for money got by bribery or graft

explanation.surface: A firm's accountant is quietly pocketing some dodgy cash.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole caboodle is the whole lot or group of things or people.
explanation.definitionFit: Caboodle, as in 'the whole caboodle', means a collection or bunch of people or things.

clue.text: Sticks close at first to Queen, we hear

indicators.note: at first means only the opening letter of the word before is taken
we hear means the name is to be judged by sound, not by its usual spelling

blocks.note: the opening letter of close
Ellery Queen, the detective-fiction author, said aloud

explanation.surface: Something clings close to the monarch, it is rumoured.
explanation.walkthrough: Queen is not the monarch but Ellery Queen, the American crime writer; spelt by sound with one L.
explanation.definitionFit: Celery is sold and eaten as sticks, the long stalks of the plant.

clue.text: Papers concealed in sofa-bed

indicators.note: concealed suggests letters disguised so the original words cannot be seen, i.e. rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Documents hidden away inside a sofa-bed.
explanation.walkthrough: It looks like a hidden word, but the letters are rearranged, not found in a row.
explanation.definitionFit: Bona fides, in informal British use, are credentials or documents proving who someone is.

clue.text: Neat bowling by man from Exeter, perhaps

definitions.note: Oxonian is also an adjective, of Oxford University

blocks.note: neat is an old word for cattle, of which an ox is one
a bowler who is bowling is said to be on
a man's name

explanation.surface: Someone from the Devon city of Exeter is bowling close by.
explanation.walkthrough: Exeter here is not the Devon city but Exeter College, Oxford, so its member is an Oxford man.
explanation.definitionFit: An Oxonian is a member of Oxford University, and Exeter is one of its colleges, hence 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Right about one not getting up

definitions.note: a phrase for the noun's state

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the right is wrapped round the number

blocks.note: a lien is a legal right to keep another's property until a debt is paid
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone correct about a person who refuses to stand.
explanation.definitionFit: A lie-in is a spell of staying in bed in the morning beyond the usual rising time.

clue.text: Missile chasing plane - it's been thrown off

indicators.note: chasing means following behind, so the missile comes after the aircraft in the answer

blocks.note: a jet is an aircraft
SAM is a surface-to-air missile

explanation.surface: A missile streaks after an aircraft, and something gets jettisoned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chasing' puts the missile after the plane, so JET comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: Jetsam is cargo deliberately cast overboard from a ship to lighten it.

clue.text: Favours disposing of our jails

indicators.note: disposing of means getting rid of, so the word our is taken out

blocks.note: to favour a cause is to encourage it
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone backs getting rid of the nation's prisons.
explanation.walkthrough: Jails is a verb here, not the plural of prison.
explanation.definitionFit: To encage something is to shut it in a cage, just as to jail someone is to lock them up.

clue.text: Fine and dandy

blocks.note: first meaning: excellent, in American slang
second meaning: a fashionably dressed man

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine and dandy' is a stock phrase, but the two words define separately: adjective and noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Swell is slang for excellent, and as a noun an elegantly dressed fashionable man.

clue.text: Young female to throw things at, getting letters wrong

blocks.note: a miss is a girl or young woman
to pelt is to hurl missiles at

explanation.surface: A girl becomes a target, with misaddressed post getting lost.
explanation.definitionFit: A word misspelt has its letters set down incorrectly, the very thing described.

clue.text: A bird that represents the devil

blocks.note: taken as written
a poll is a parrot
yon is an old word for that, as in yon hill

explanation.surface: A bird stands as a symbol of the devil.
explanation.walkthrough: Apollyon is the destroying angel of Revelation, and the fiend Christian fights in Pilgrim's Progress.
explanation.definitionFit: Apollyon is a Biblical name for Satan, the destroyer from the bottomless pit.

clue.text: Corruptly keep clients on so as to appropriate their money

indicators.note: something done corruptly is twisted out of its proper form, so the words following get reworked

blocks.note: the fodder, every letter used

explanation.surface: A crooked adviser strings clients along so as to siphon off their savings.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram indicator 'Corruptly' also suits the definition, which is about dishonest enrichment.
explanation.definitionFit: To line one's pockets is to enrich oneself, usually dishonestly, from funds entrusted to one.

clue.text: Desperado going around in green coat

indicators.note: going around means turning back on itself, so the words that follow are read from the end

blocks.note: naif means naive, inexperienced
an animal's coat is its fur

explanation.surface: An outlaw on the run is wearing a green overcoat.
explanation.walkthrough: Green is the inexperienced sense, not a colour, and 'going around' turns the whole two-word string back to front.
explanation.definitionFit: A desperado is a reckless criminal, and a ruffian is a violent lawless person: near synonyms.

clue.text: Cricketer stages a display of cheek

blocks.note: the stages of a journey are its legs
lip is impudent talk, cheek

explanation.surface: A performer puts on a show of impudence.
explanation.walkthrough: Leg slip is a close fielding position behind the batsman on the leg side, and by extension the fielder there.
explanation.definitionFit: The fielder placed at leg slip is a cricketer named after that position on the field.

clue.text: I make an impression if, when speaking. I empathise

indicators.note: when speaking means the string of words is to be said out loud and heard as one word

blocks.clueFragment: I make an impression if, when speaking. I
blocks.note: make an impression is DENT, and the words run together as I-dent-if-I

explanation.surface: Someone describes how, by sharing feelings, they leave a mark.
explanation.walkthrough: Say 'I dent if I' quickly and it is the answer; dent is an impression.
explanation.definitionFit: To identify with someone is to feel along with them, which is what empathising means.

clue.text: Water plant needs heated environment

indicators.note: an environment is surroundings, so the heated word surrounds the plant

blocks.note: heated in temper, angry
a rig is industrial plant, e.g. a drilling rig

explanation.surface: A water plant needs a warm greenhouse to grow.
explanation.walkthrough: Water looks like a noun beside plant, but it is the verb, and the plant is machinery.
explanation.definitionFit: To irrigate land is to supply it with water through channels or pipes.

clue.text: Some bloomer! A dreadful lapse!

indicators.note: something dreadful is in a terrible state, so the word that follows is badly jumbled

blocks.note: the fodder

explanation.surface: An exclamation at a howling blunder: what an awful slip!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomer' looks like a blunder, but it is a flowering plant, and a sepal is one part of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A sepal is part of a flower's calyx, so it is a piece of something that blooms.

clue.text: Play pawn first  that's commonplace

indicators.note: first places the chess piece ahead of the other part rather than after it

blocks.note: P is the chess notation for pawn
play in a mechanism, freedom of movement

explanation.surface: Opening with a pawn move is a routine, unoriginal chess move.
explanation.definitionFit: A platitude is a trite remark, and a commonplace is likewise a hackneyed saying.

clue.text: Scattered raid goes wrong  police upset about it

indicators.note: goes wrong means the word raid is put into a faulty order
upset in a down clue means turned over, so the police word is read bottom to top
about it means wrapped around the mixed-up raid

blocks.note: cops are police officers
the fodder

explanation.surface: A police raid goes awry and the force is in uproar.
explanation.definitionFit: Sporadic means occurring at irregular intervals or in isolated places, so scattered.

clue.text: Whale that's caught by ship, a steamer

indicators.note: caught by means held inside the words that follow, which enclose the letters wanted

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of one word and into the next two

explanation.surface: A whale gets caught by a ship, a steamship.
explanation.walkthrough: Whale is a verb here, to beat soundly, not the sea creature.
explanation.definitionFit: To paste someone is to thrash them, and to whale is likewise to beat hard: verb synonyms.

clue.text: Message giving directions about round missing from gun

indicators.note: missing from means the round shape is absent from the weapon
about means the compass points go around the rest

blocks.note: two compass points, east and east
O is round in shape
a pistol is a handgun

explanation.surface: A note giving instructions about a gun with a missing bullet.
explanation.walkthrough: Round reads as a bullet, but it is just the letter shaped like a circle.
explanation.definitionFit: An epistle is a letter, especially a formal one, and so a written message.

clue.text: Peel invested a lot of money once in a solution to traffic problems

indicators.note: a lot of means most but not all, so the final letter of the coin is dropped
invested means clothed or wrapped, so the peel wraps around the money

blocks.note: peel is the rind of fruit
the groat was an old English fourpenny coin

explanation.surface: Sir Robert Peel once sank a fortune into a scheme to ease congestion.
explanation.walkthrough: Peel looks like the Prime Minister, but it is fruit skin; the groat was an old English fourpenny coin, so 'a lot of' trims its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A ring road circles a town so that through traffic avoids the congested centre.

clue.text: From the outset, regular employment beat being out of work

indicators.note: from the outset means only the opening letters of the next words are used

blocks.note: the first letters of regular and employment
beat means exhausted

explanation.surface: Steady work from the start beats being unemployed.
explanation.walkthrough: Beat is an adjective, worn out, not a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone retired has given up their job for good and so is no longer working.

clue.text: Angler trapped by rising river washed away

indicators.note: rising in a down clue means read from the bottom upwards
trapped by means held inside, so the angler sits within the river

blocks.note: the Dee is a British river
an angler is a rod in the sense of a fisherman

explanation.surface: A fisherman caught out by a flooding river is swept away.
explanation.definitionFit: Eroded land has been worn down, often by water carrying the soil off.

clue.text: Making fun of a woman singer

blocks.note: Eve was made from Adam's rib, so a rib is jocularly a woman or wife
Bing Crosby, the crooner

explanation.surface: Someone mocks a female vocalist.
explanation.walkthrough: Rib for a woman is an old joke from Genesis.
explanation.definitionFit: To rib someone is to tease them good-humouredly, so ribbing means teasing or mocking.

clue.text: Derby loses money in recess

indicators.note: loses means the hat is without the symbol for money

blocks.note: a derby is the American name for a bowler hat
L is the pound sign, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: A Derby horse race loses money during a break.
explanation.walkthrough: Derby is the hat, not the horse race.
explanation.definitionFit: A bower is a shady retreat or nook in a garden, so a sheltered recess.

clue.text: Wanting more food and more game

blocks.note: first meaning: greedier, from gutsy as gluttonous
second meaning: braver, game meaning plucky

explanation.surface: A diner keen for another helping and more venison.
explanation.walkthrough: Game reads as meat on the menu, but here it means willing and brave.
explanation.definitionFit: Gutsy means both greedy for food and courageous, so its comparative carries both senses.

clue.text: English composer about to get the bird

indicators.note: about here means turned round, so the whole is read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: E for English
Alban Berg, the Austrian composer

explanation.surface: An English composer is about to receive the bird, being booed off.
explanation.walkthrough: Getting the bird means being jeered, but here it is the actual bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The grebe is a diving water bird, such as the great crested grebe.

clue.text: Qualified now to end drought completely

indicators.note: qualified means modified or altered, so the words that follow are changed in order

blocks.note: the fodder, every letter used

explanation.surface: A forecaster hedges about the rain finally ending the dry spell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down to the ground' is usually heard in 'suits me down to the ground'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom down to the ground means thoroughly or entirely, as in 'it suits me' that way.

clue.text: The action of a bounder and a cad. O.K.?

blocks.note: a cur is a contemptible man
to vet is to check and pass as OK

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a rotter's behaviour is acceptable.
explanation.walkthrough: A bounder seems to be a cad, but here it is a horse that bounds; a curvet is a leap in dressage.
explanation.definitionFit: A curvet is a horse's leap with the forelegs raised, the movement of an animal that bounds.

clue.text: One who's not paid to work in the garden

blocks.note: first meaning: a person admitted or carried free, without a ticket
second meaning: to snip off withered flowers

explanation.surface: An unpaid volunteer doing the gardening.
explanation.walkthrough: A deadhead is one who has not paid, such as a free-ticket holder; read 'not paid' as unwaged and you go astray.
explanation.definitionFit: Deadhead is a non-paying passenger or spectator, and as a verb it means removing faded blooms from plants.
